utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So Madam Registrar, good morning to you. Could you kindly call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-05-88-T, the Prosecutor versus Vujadin Popovic et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Everyone is here except Mr. Bourgon. Prosecution we have Mr. McCloskey back, and Mr. Thayer and Mr. Vanderpuye. You would have noticed this morning that we are missing Judge -- Reserve Judge Stole. That will happen again tomorrow. So we will be invoking the provisions of Rule 15 bis and proceeding accordingly in his absence. We had left unfinished the matter of tendering of documents, Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. Good morning to you and Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let me see, because I think my secretary --

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I -- I think under the press of time, Your Honour, we had pretty much held up the exhibit list and asked generally if there were any objections. There is one modification with respect to PIC00040, and that would be the Prosecution's request to place that under seal. And that is the third exhibit up from the bottom of the list, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You need to refresh our memory of what that document is.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Yes. That is the B/C/S version of the intercept dated 14 July 1995 at 2102 hours marked by the witness during his testimony on 22 November.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And you want it under seal?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And there is an objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: No, there is not, but we had not indicated that we wished to place that under seal on that exhibit list previously.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. I heard the word objection. Madam Registrar is drawing our attention to the fact that that may be also the case of putting under seal also the next two documents, 41 and 42 from the notebook.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: That would be a good idea, Your Honour, out of an abundance of caution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ostojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President and Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I'm just not sure why we are placing it under seal. The three pages that are at issue are IC00040, 41, and 42. 42 is the only one that bears a signature apparently of the protected witness; the other two pages do not. They were just markings. I would just like to know the basis of why he wishes that the two pages that do not bear any signature, why they require that to be under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer. If we see them -- if we see them it will help us understand better, if we have a look at them. I mean, I suppose they can be easily found.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Again, they are PIC00040.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The thing is -- I think my memory is coming back. We are talking of this same intercept in all three cases to start with, and that intercept is signed, I think, if I remember well, by the witness. So irrespective of whether you're referring to one or more parts of it, if you leave the end part -- or if you leave the entire document or parts of it not under seal, anyone can make two and two together, refer to the intercept by date and time, because we have date and time, and be able to trace it back to the -- to the witness, because there is the -- his signature at the end of it. This is what I mean. I have 40. Say if we put only 40 under seal, okay, the rest of the evidence which is not in private session and which refers to that document would ultimately reveal his identity. So I think the whole -- the whole statement -- or the whole intercept should be under seal that whole intercept.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I don't want to belabour the point, but I thought it was in open session when I questioned this witness on the first two pages, and only the third page bears the witnesses signature, so I'm not sure how with in excess of 140 logbooks but I just wanted to know the basis for it. If that's what it is, we'll accept that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Questioning him and answering questions on that document is one thing. Making the document available is another. In other words, the testimony in open session as it relates to that document provided that document is kept under seal is harmless. It won't expose his identity. While if in -- you let parts of that document be available to the public, then his handwriting is made available, his name could be made available. So it's putting -- putting the jigsaw together that could identify. So I think it's better to play it safe and have it -- have it under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Yes, let's put it all -- the entire document under seal, please. You have the list. You told me last Friday that this -- the list of intended exhibits was handed to you. Is there any objection from any of the Defence teams, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. We have sent a list of documents to the Bench. These are documents that we used during cross-examination of the previous witness. I don't think there's any need for me to repeat the documents again because you have them in written form. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Is there any objection on the Prosecution's part?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Your Honour, unfortunately we've not received that list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It was around last Friday. I'm sure you have received it, because it was circulating last Friday.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Is it just the list of exhibits that were used now being offered as tendered? Okay. I understand now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I know it was circulated last Friday and my impression is that it crossed the floor. Okay. But it shouldn't be difficult. Let's give you our decision. In view of the general objection that has been raised by the Defence teams as to the admissibility of intercepts, all intercepts that are being sought to be tendered following the testimony of the gentleman we had with us last week, instead of being admitted now will be marked for identification along the lines that we explained to you when we first started the trial. Ultimately, eventually we will decide on their admissibility, the final admissibility or not. So I don't think we need, Madam Registrar, to waste time to identify which is an intercept and which is not. I think you can do that, and you can receive assistance, I suppose, from the Prosecution and then check it out which the parties. That applies both ways, because you have also made use, of course, of some of these intercepts, but that will not be held against you because -- because you have this general objection. So -- but all intercepts will be marked for identification for the time being. All right? Understood. All right. Yes, Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sorry. One just -- just one matter of clarification. If you take a look at the Prosecution's list of exhibits to tender, given our prior discussion I just wanted to make clear that with respect to P01164, it is the entire packet that the Prosecution seeks to place under seal for the same reasons that Your Honour just pointed out, in addition to the final printout also bearing his name in typed form. The way it's printed here might just be a little misleading in that it may seem to go to that last printout incept or we intend or we seek to admit the entire packet under seal. I just wanted to make that clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's clear enough.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. I think we can close this matter here. It stands to reason that all other exhibits which are not intercepts coming from both sides are hereby admitted. Yes. I noticed Madam Nikolic first.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There is one document which remains unclear to me whether the Prosecution tendered it. This is P02312. This is a set of working reports that were presented to the witness during examination. This document is not contained on the exhibit list for this witness. It was added during the examination-in-chief of the witness. In the course of our cross-examination, I used page 20 of the document. I would like to tender the document or, rather, the page into evidence. However, if my learned friend wishes to tender the entire document, then there is no need for me to do this. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Madam Nikolic, I think if -- at least in the list that I have, that I was given -- that we were given last Friday, it is there. It's between -- it's the last one before the IC PIC documents.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is possible, because I don't have the -- my notes from Friday here. 2308 is the last document according to myself, to my notes. If that's correct, then --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: There's also P02312. All right? So that settles the matter. I had recognised Mr. Ostojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. With respect to the packet of printed materials, it was my understanding that the Court requested that the Prosecution also provide prior dates in addition to the one -- the 15th, because only the 14th was there. So I would object only on the grounds that I haven't -- maybe they've produced it, but I haven't seen that yet. So in accordance with that. And also just for clarification if the Court -- although you say we tender -- will accept, admit all documents, we specifically just want to clarify for the record that we wanted Exhibit 2D38 admitted and also Exhibit which was previously marked as 3D31 and now I think we call it by the new name 2D3D31, which is the May 1999 information sheet from the Office of the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. I take it there is no objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: There is no objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: As regards the other, you said the Trial Chamber requested. We didn't request. We asked Mr. McCloskey at the time whether he thought it would be more helpful if he brought all -- along also the 13th July intercepts if they existed, and he did say that he was trying to get them over, but I don't think we can -- yes. I don't think that we can say we requested them, and I don't think that there was an undertaking, specific undertaking on the part of the Prosecution which rather acknowledged at the time that this could be more confusing. I couldn't see how it could be more confusing, but Mr. McCloskey, on the eve of Thanksgiving, thought it was confusing. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think at the time that -- that that offer was -- was brought up again, frankly it appeared that we'd all suffered enough with the exposition with P02312. We do have the -- the packet for the 13th available, and we can make it available to the Bench.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But I don't think --

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I think that ship has sailed, frankly, Your Honour, but we do have it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The three of us don't think it is necessary at this stage. So the other two documents that have been mentioned by Mr. Ostojic, of course, are also -- also admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And this packet is being translated, isn't it? 2312.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: We -- we haven't submitted it in its entirety but -- because the substance of the intercepts wasn't at issue. If there are portions that were discussed during the testimony, of course we will make those -- we will have those translated. If the Court wishes the entire packet to be translated, then we can of course submit it for translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Let's try to simplify it. What we need translated is in -- in each case from these typed transcripts in B/C/S we need translated the material at the top above the line and the material immediately following beneath the line before the actual transcript begins. All right? For example, in the first one you have the indication of the megahertz, the channel, and the time. Then you have "Pravac - JI," and "UCC:XY." That's all we need to have translated. But it will -- you need to cover that through the entire document. For example, in the second one beneath the line there is also the words "very urgent" on the right. We need to have those reproduced, not translated, and so on. Have you understood? Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I believe I've understood you well, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thanks. Thanks a lot. Thank you, Judge Kwon. Can we -- is there any preliminary business you wish to raise? Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes. Good morning, Mr. President and everyone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I just wanted to make a -- make a motion, it's a joint motion that the Defence and the Prosecution are all very much together on, and that is that the week of February -- Monday, February 12th be a week off for us to be able to organise ourselves and catch our breath. That will be important, because it is our plan to bring in the expert archaeologists and anthropologists and pathologists on the week of February 19th and they're coming from all over the world. So having a good idea of an exact time and some time to prepare for that would be helpful, and I know the Defence would like this time as well. And it's important for our scheduling purposes. We're scheduling enough in advance and we need to know which week -- and these weeks, as you know, have been very helpful for everyone because everyone has been working very hard. And in fact we would look to March even for our scheduling purposes, and the Defence joins this also, that the week of Monday, March 26th would also be a good week to take. That would be the next 30 days after this break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So I take it this has already been sort of discussed and agreed upon by the two sides. We do appreciate that you have been working very hard, both of you, both Prosecution and Defence, and that as we had indicated in the beginning of the trial, we are -- we are conscious that periodically there will be required some time off for reorganising the ranks. But let us think about it and we'll come back to you in the day or latest tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I understand that the week of the 25th of March is required by -- 26th of March is required by the Defence. Can any one spokesman for the Defence at least indicate what the reason is?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I'm not sure, Your Honour, if this is the precise reason. I think when we met with Mr. McCloskey we were scheduling approximately 4 to 6 weeks, and anticipating that the 12th would be granted we just looked into March, and then he said, "What do you think about March?" And we picked the last week in March. There was nothing more specific than that with respect to that scheduling. We just wanted it to be 4 to 6 weeks from the last break. That was basically our logic in that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. I thank you. And you confirm this, Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. And I think the logic in some of -- there was some family issues, children and things.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. We'll come back to you, as I stated. We need to discuss that amongst ourselves. So can we bring in the witness. No. I think I need to explain to the general public that we are drawing the curtains down for the time being because we are bringing in a protected witness, so you cannot see him entering the courtroom, but after that we'll lift -- and we'll soon be in open session again very soon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think you can lift the curtains, Madam Usher, please. Thank you, Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning to you, sir, and welcome to this Tribunal and to this case which deals with the events in Srebrenica in July of 1995. You are about to start giving evidence, but before you do so our rules require that you make a solemn declaration undertaking to testify to the truth. The text is being handed to you. Please read it out aloud and that will be your undertaking with us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Please make yourself comfortable. Take a seat. I suppose you are aware that we have put in place by way of protecting your identity three protective measures, namely, the use of a pseudonym instead of your real name, and you are going to be referred to as PW-131 - is that correct, 131? - and we are also -- we have also put in place both visual and voice distortion. I suppose this has been explained to you by the Victims and Witnesses Unit. What I would like to know if this is so and, secondly, whether this is to your satisfaction.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. You have to speak into that special microphone that you have in front of you as we go along. There will be moments that we will go in private session. In other words, what is being said will only be heard inside this courtroom and not beyond its walls, but we'll try to limit that as much as possible. Mr. Vanderpuye will go first. He will then be cross-examined by -- you will then be cross-examined by the various Defence teams. You have given testimony already in other proceedings, and Mr. Vanderpuye will be dealing with that matter in the beginning of his intervention. Yes, Mr. Vanderpuye, he's all yours.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President, Your Honours, ladies and gentlemen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning. Could you also tell us -- give us an indication of how long you expect to be examining your witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I would estimate somewhere in the neighbourhood of about an hour and half to maybe two hours. I had intended to follow up on certain issues identified by the witness's prior testimony that I think are relevant to these proceedings and will be helpful to the Court in its determination of these issues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Just an indication. And, Madam Registrar, have you obtained from the Defence teams an indication of how long they expect? If -- perhaps Mr. Zivanovic can deal with that. If you can circulate a piece of paper and then let us know. Give -- have an indication so that we can plan for the rest of the week. In the meantime, I think we can start, Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I also wanted to indicate to the Court that I had intended at some point during the further examination of this witness to use a map. It's a physical map, rather big. I don't believe that there's an exact replica on e-court. I think part of it is in e-court. But I just wanted to use it for demonstrative purposes in order to assist the Court and also the witness in terms of conveying some relevant aspects of his testimony. The other thing that I would like to bring to the Court's attention is that the transcript of the witness's prior testimony refers to certain exhibits. The exhibits were not tendered in relation to that testimony, but I had intended to offer them with respect to his testimony here today. I don't know whether or not Defence has an objection to that, but that would be the -- the idea.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I hear no objection, so I understand we can proceed along those lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: If I may begin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. The sooner the better.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Madam Usher, please show the witness the pseudonym sheet, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Sir, please have a look at that document, P0230 -- P02310. Have a look at that, and without telling us what's on the document, can you tell us whether or not you're the person named in it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-131
utterances.text: Yes. It contains my name and PW-131.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... reminding me that you have your microphone on. It should be off when the witness is speaking. So just to make sure, I just don't like taking risks, we block the transmission of this last part, this very last minute or few seconds before I intervened. Just the transmission, that's all. Please be careful, all of us, not to keep the microphone on when the witness is speaking.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: For the purposes of the 92 ter procedure, I would like to read a summary of the witness's prior testimony and for that I would ask if we can perhaps go into private session because it deals with a lot of sensitive issues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Let's go into private session for a short while. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are in open session. Thank you, Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Can you tell the Court what type of equipment was used in your unit?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-131
utterances.text: Your Honours, we had absolutely no military equipment. That is to say, that all of the equipment was procured through friendly contacts, through friends. So we mostly had civilian equipment from radio amateur clubs, ham radio clubs. We would take that equipment, make some adjustments, and then use it for our purposes, which turned out to be quite useful. Initially we had several RUP 12 devices used by companies or platoons. It was very difficult to use them because the system for surveillance using them is quite complicated. So our resources were really pitiful. As I told you earlier, we had absolutely no resources to follow civilian communications which go above 900 or 1000 megahertz.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Do you recall, for example, what types of transceivers were employed in the unit in and around 1995?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-131
utterances.text: Yes, I do remember. Those were mostly devices produced by Collins, JVC and others.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: In addition to the technical equipment, did you use physical tapes?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-131
utterances.text: Yes. The situation was a bit unusual regarding the tapes. Since all of the channels for procuring equipment had been shut down, most of our tapes originated from Radio Tuzla station, which means that they had been in use for over 10 years, maybe even more. I remember that it was only in 1996 that we received the first set containing 10 tapes. In addition, recording devices, UHER, at the time used only by journalists were the ones that we received from radio stations in Tuzla, Lukavac, Banovici, wherever we were able to find them. We didn't have a single military piece of equipment in our unit. We constructed all of the antennas by ourselves from traffic signs, plastic sewage pipes, using copper. That's what we used.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: You'd indicated before that some modifications were made to the radio equipment in order to -- in order that they be used effectively. Can you tell us what those modifications were, if you know?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-131
utterances.text: Buying the equipment that had been procured before the war in the civilian world, all ham radio equipment had only a certain range within which they functioned. Military frequencies had a different range, a totally different range. So we would make a simple modification, adjustment, and we would expand the band, thus adjusting these pieces of equipment to military frequencies. In this case, we did it so that we could follow communications on RRU 800, which used exclusively analogue system. It was very easy to follow these communications. Then we also used this for a newer piece of equipment, RRU 1, which was also easy to monitor, and a piece of equipment known as HVT, FM-200. Similarly, we made modifications on antennas to make adjustments for certain ranges. Initially we used just plain TV antennas. Later on, we constructed more flexible antennas that could cover a broader range. People doing this did it for two reasons. In order to defend themselves; that was the first reason. And the other reason, let me to be frank again, in order not to go into combat. They had to produce a valuable result so that they wouldn't be sent to combat. After all, they were much safer. Their lives were much safer in these facilities than at the front. Whoever worked there was either a ham radio operator or somebody who did that in the former JNA. I always used to say that it would have been better for the JNA and VRS to have used civilian communications than the ones that they actually used, because that technology was over 30 years old. This means that they had certain protected or encrypted channels, but they used it infrequently mostly, and we were unable to follow that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Well, in terms of the capabilities of the unit, and maybe you'll correct me if I'm wrong, are you suggesting that the unit didn't have the capacity to monitor these civilian lines of communication?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-131
utterances.text: Yes. Given that the SMC pieces of equipment mostly used by civilians and during wartime - sometimes the army used it too - we were unable to monitor those frequencies because we were unable to make modifications on our equipment in order for it to be used on these frequencies, because they used a different technical approach. It's a bit complicated for me to explain it to you, but let me just say that the ham radio equipment that we had was not capable of monitoring these frequencies.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: With respect to the frequencies that you were capable of monitoring, did the VRS engage in tactics in order to avoid having these communications intercepted, such as terrain masking or things of that nature?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-131
utterances.text: From my point of view, this is something that should have existed in all armies. The advantage we had -- what gave us the advantage is that they had precisely that type of equipment. In addition, ABiH army also had the advantage of not possessing any equipment. Otherwise, they would have been monitoring our communications too. Officers at lower levels mostly abided by radio communication regulations, whereas higher-level officers disregarded them. And it was precisely from these persons that we gathered most of our data. They probably only looked towards the end of the war, and they never tried to conceal their goals.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: When you say they never tried to conceal their goals, can I ask you, in your experience did the VRS broadcast, for example, at minimum power from these relay stations, or did they broadcast it more than what was necessary in order to relay a given communication?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-131
utterances.text: The army of Republika Srpska used to the maximum radio relay communications, especially when it came to combat operations, in which case they used RRU 1, which was transportable easily. They could go anywhere where they did not have an energy supply and install it there. In this case, they installed this radio relay equipment in Pribicevac above Srebrenica in January of 1995. They installed it in the middle of a forest, and they planned to do something. We were able to uncover this quite soon.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: In general, can you tell us whether or not your unit --

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Can we go into private session for a moment?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Certainly, Mr. Vanderpuye. Private session, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Did your unit have any relationship with the 21st Division of the ABiH?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-131
utterances.text: In the command sense we had absolutely no links with them. We had nothing to do with the 21st Division. As for cooperation, yes, we did cooperate, but we never used the same equipment. They sent all of their reports to the command of the 21st Division. Their first and main task was to monitor communications of the army of Republika Srpska in the part of Bosnia called Posavina. That is to say, from Modrica to Bijeljina.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Was there any overlap between the area that that unit covered versus the area that yours covered?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-131
utterances.text: Certainly. We had horizontal coordination. For example, if something came up near Olovo or, say, in Srebrenica, we would ask for assistance from that same unit, because we had, for example, one piece of equipment, one UHER, and we could only follow one channel with it. That was the regular procedure. I'm trying to bring your attention to the fact that in addition to the platoon and the 21st Division we had platoons in other divisions, 24th, 22nd, 25th Division, and they all covered certain areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Was there any sharing of information or intercepts between your unit and the 21st?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-131
utterances.text: Yes. As I said a bit earlier, it was a regular procedure. For example, we would say, "We're interested in the channel, in this particular channel. Can you give us this information?" And since we were quite close, if we were busy working on one channel, we would tell them, "Why don't you monitor this other channel?"

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Can we go into private session for one second?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Certainly. Let's go into private session for a while.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: It's actually a perfect time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We'll have a 30-minute break starting from now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So we are in open session. We have the map stuck to the screen. You also said previously, Mr. Vanderpuye, that at least part of it is on e-court. It may become important to have it available in that manner as well, because we will be able at least to zoom into parts of it. All right. You may proceed. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. My information is actually the entire map is on e-court. It's just enormous and takes a tremendous amount of time to load, and my suggestion was at some point maybe to refer to a smaller area of it so as to make it more convenient for everybody.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We can always -- let's be practical about it. If that is the case, we can always have copies made of the interesting parts of that map which we can put on the ELMO, and we can zoom in on those as well, or put those selected parts on e-court in addition to what we have already, and we can utilise that facility better then. All right?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Good afternoon -- good morning. Good morning, Mr. Witness. Could you tell us with respect to the work protocol at your unit, during the course of actually transcribing an intercept was it the case that more than one person could or would listen to a given communication?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Your mic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Under the work protocol there, was the possibility for one person to listening in to a conversation or for several persons to listen in. The latter method served to make sure that you did not miss out on something, and it also depended on the way the people worked. (redacted)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We need to redact this last sentence, please. Witness, please. I mean, I don't need to stay repeating this. Please refrain from mentioning the names of any of the sites, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Did you -- did you have the ability to receive or -- receive corroborative information with respect to the intercepts that were being taken down or transcribed within your unit?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-131
utterances.text: Well, this may be a bit difficult to explain. However, the situation on the ground indicated -- or, rather, proved the veracity of these conversations. We knew of every attack by the VRS ahead of time. We were able to confirm the information received through the events on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: With respect to the intercept operators that were working at the -- working within the unit, were you aware of whether or not or to what degree their prior training had been or they had received?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-131
utterances.text: For the most part the people coming into the unit were ham radio operators or persons who were engaged in these activities in the JNA. We provided some degree of training at the workplace, and these people had to meet certain requirements. There had to have been a recommendation to the effect that a given person was specialised in that activity. In my unit I had top-notch mathematicians, mechanical engineers, and there were people coming from different backgrounds.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: With respect to the organisation of the unit, were platoon commanders trained intercept operators?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-131
utterances.text: Every platoon commander, in addition to holding that post, was an operator and did the job just as all the other persons did. That person would coordinate the work taking place in a room. If one frequency was occupied, then he would instruct another operator to go on and monitor another frequency.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And in terms of the monitoring of frequencies, as long as we're talking about that, by what authority, if any, were given frequencies monitored within the unit?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-131
utterances.text: Every job of work was done on the basis of an order. Orders specified in detail the zones to be intercepted from one facility and the zones to be intercepted by another facility. On the basis of the information, the unit command decided whether a facility was to assist in intercepting communications. For instance, if the communications to be intercepted took place in the south, then we decided which facility would be covering that, whether that would be the one in the north. For instance, our facility in the north had consistent tasks to cover communications ranging from Banja Luka all the way down to Zvornik, whereas the facility in the south was to cover the communications from Zvornik all the way down to Rogatica or Han Pijesak in the south. That was their basic task.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Well, did the platoon commanders assist other intercept operators in either the analysis or transcription of particular or given communications?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-131
utterances.text: Yes. Every commander was the first filter for data analysis. They had their aide-memoires where they would write down the features of a communication, the persons participating in it, and the contents. Let me point out that at no point in time did the -- one commander know which communications were being intercepted at the other facility and vice versa. These processes were kept quite separate.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: In terms of data analysis, did these commanders help in the identification of persons, locations, resources, things of those -- things of that nature that was -- were the subject of a given intercept communication?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-131
utterances.text: Yes, of course. This was auxiliary material helping us in our work without which we would not have been able to work properly or draw proper conclusions. In addition the intercepting activities, every commander would have a given time to search the bands. The first and foremost task was to designate a code-name for all the activities and to fill in all the gaps. For instance, participants in the communications. We knew who Panorama 1, Panorama 2, or Panorama 3 were. What posed the greatest difficulty to us was when these code-names changed. In addition to that, all the members of the unit and department were well aware of the features of every person, what sort of accents they used who were their most frequent contents, what the names of their children and wife were, who answered the phone for them, and every person had a dossier which contained only the data collected through monitoring.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Now, when you refer to this body of information and the data, is that -- well, was that information available to intercept operators working within your unit for the purposes of analysis and processing, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-131
utterances.text: Naturally. These lads had been doing the job for three years. They were on top of what they were doing, and they had no trouble recognising and identifying persons. What's more, they would work together and, if need be, they would listen to the tape for 20 times, time and again, in order to recognise the person. We weren't interested so much in who was speaking as we were in what they were talking about. This was the next point. We were supposed to accurately convey the words uttered, i.e., the information obtained.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: With respect to the development of the information that was relied upon by the intercept operators in performing their function, were there meetings that were held with regard to the development or analysis of this information?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-131
utterances.text: Within the unit we carried out a series of analyses. One analysis was taking place in all the facilities every 10 days where the main focus of the forthcoming period was designated, as were the activities. We also had a small analysis section within our unit at our facility, and we held briefings once weekly. There were persons whose only job was to enter features of certain -- or attributes of certain persons and other information concerning these persons for days, so that we were able to uncover their chain of command simply on the basis of intercepting these conversations. We knew which person hid behind which number.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Now, you'd indicated that part of the information that was developed in part by your unit included the code-names for certain locations; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-131
utterances.text: Yes. This was the first and main task we had, to -- to uncover the location, unit, or a person behind a certain code-name.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: With respect to the reliability of the information that was developed by your unit, can you tell us what the unit's responsibility to the headquarters was in terms of the timeliness of the information that was conveyed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-131
utterances.text: I wouldn't wish to discuss the reliability of information. I told you already that our main task was to accurately convey the information recorded. We provided our assessment of reliability at our level, which was then double-checked at a higher level, at the corps command. In view of the events that had transpired in the previous three years, we were able to assess what the actual events on the grounds would be.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned that the information that was conveyed by your unit was double-checked at the corps command. May I ask, did you ever receive any complaints or concerns with respect to the information that was furnished by your unit?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-131
utterances.text: As far as I remember, I never received any complaints or concerns. Quite the contrary. We were commended for our work.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: May I go into private session for a moment, Mr. President?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Certain information was sent from your unit to the higher command in Tuzla, and you've indicated that that information was then analysed a second time. And could you tell us, if you know, was that particular analysis done by a dedicated unit?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-131
utterances.text: As I've said already, the first analysis was done within the unit by drawing upon -- on the information received through intercepting alone. The next step of analysis was done in the intelligence department where they got information from elsewhere, from captured persons and informants, and all the information converged to this one point.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Now, with respect to the information that was conveyed by your unit to the higher command, was that information conveyed electronically?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-131
utterances.text: The information from both facilities, once they were produced in their final form on the computer, was sent on through a protected radio package. From the north facility we had the wire device, whereas we did not have one in the southern facility, and that's why the paket communication was used on a daily basis with encryption.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: With respected to the sending of encrypted information, was that -- was that done by a person that was qualified within the unit to do so?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-131
utterances.text: Yes. We had a communications platoon as part of our unit. The persons manning this package system had to go through special training and they had to take an oath, a confidentiality oath, and persons holding such qualifications would be sent to apposite facilities. They had their own rooms to which only the platoon commander and other authorised persons had access.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: With respect to the information that they sent, the electronic information, I should be more specific, are you familiar with how that information is sent from the site to the headquarters?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-131
utterances.text: Of course I'm familiar with that. First of all, we would receive from the superior command every month a key, a password for every day, and only the information obtained on a given date could be sent, passed on on that same day. So that all the information typed out in the original form was sent encoded to the relevant organ in Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: With respect to the information that was typed out and sent, can you tell us where that information was derived from?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-131
utterances.text: For the most part the information received was typed out from notebooks that were previously filled up by listening to the taped reels. This was hard work and time-consuming, but we didn't have any other working method.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Now, the notebooks that you're referring to, are those otherwise known as daily logs?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-131
utterances.text: These were just ordinary notebooks. Every such station should by its structure have a station logbook, but we didn't have such formats of logs because they were in short supply. We had to use regular notebooks. Quite a few such notebooks were actually incinerated because there had been no obligation to store these notebooks for a given time. They would be disposed of as soon as the information from them had been conveyed onto a computer. We were in the middle of a forest. We also needed firewood.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: "In the middle of a mountain."

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: With respect to the notebooks in particular, can you tell us who, if anyone, was responsible for distributing and/or collecting these notebooks?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-131
utterances.text: I've already said there was no requirement by law to save those notebooks. The procedure was as follows: Whenever there was a shift working in a facility, we would bring paginated, new notebooks. We would take those that had been filled up and take them back to the unit command.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: With respect to tapes, reel-to-reel tapes, can you tell us what the procedure was with respect to that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-131
utterances.text: Reel tapes presented the greatest problem for us, for the simple reason that we were isolated for three years. We were unable to procure reels, and we had a short supply of them. So as soon as they were recorded, we would take them to Tuzla where there was a unit which would listen to the tapes. Let me just remind you that in order to hear one tape, one side only, one needed four hours. Listening to the conversations they would set aside those which in their view were important. Then they erased those tapes and sent blank tapes back to the unit. Occasionally, due to the volume of work, they had no time to erase them, so that the tapes would be sent back to the facility with the original material still recorded on them.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Can you tell us who was responsible for collecting and/or distributing the tapes?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-131
utterances.text: It was mostly I who was present when each shift came. I would distribute tapes. I would assign tasks and convey those that we had received from the superior command. I did that unless I had some other business to attend to.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: May we go into private session for a moment?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Certainly. Let's go into private session for a while, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I would at this point like to have 65 ter number 1072 shown to the witness following the procedure prescribed by Your Honour. That's fine just where it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Can you see that, Mr. Witness?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-131
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Can I draw your attention to what is designated number 3 on that page?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-131
utterances.text: It says: "Annex number 3, review of diskettes 1.44 Mb with data collected by electronic reconnaissance of communications. Seven pieces."

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Now, was that information that was turned over by your unit to the Office of the Prosecutor on the date that's indicated on the top of that document of 13 December 2000?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-131
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And did you compile that information?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-131
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And is the information relating to what's on the diskettes consistent with and in addition to the information that was furnished back in May of 1999 in the form of two diskettes?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-131
utterances.text: Yes. The diskettes accompanied logbooks and reports printed on printers.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Now, with respect to the information or even the physical items that were turned over to the Office of the Prosecutor, did you assist in preparing those items or furnishing those items to the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-131
utterances.text: On behalf of the chief of G-2, I was tasked with handing over this material related to electronic surveillance data.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: You'd indicated -- it appears from the transcript that you've indicated that the diskettes accompanied logbooks and reports printed on printers. I see that on page 51; I think it's line 12 and 13. Let me just ask: The reference to logbooks, are you talking about logbooks separate and apart from the notebooks or inclusive of the notebooks?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-131
utterances.text: Logbooks are actually notebooks, one and the same thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Ostojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I apologise for interrupting, Your Honour, but my learned friend referenced page 51, line 12, which starts really with a question, and I don't know if we got an answer to the last question. It would seem to be an answer that they're one and the same thing, but I think the question was whether they were included with the diskettes or not in this chain of custody issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think the witness said logbooks are actually notebooks, one and the same thing. So I think he's provided an answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I followed that part. The question -- if I may, the question I thought was whether the logbooks or notebooks accompanied the diskettes, and we were examining this exhibit in front of us which talks about these diskettes. I don't think that he answered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No. I don't read it the same way as you do, but I'll block this and go back to his question, to Mr. Vanderpuye's question. You've indicated, it appears -- from the transcript that you've indicated that the diskettes accompanied logbooks and reports printed on printers. I see that on page 51; I think it's lines 12 and 13. Let me just ask -- now we come to the question. Let me just ask: The reference to logbooks, are you talking about logbooks separate and apart of the notebooks or inclusive of the notebooks? And his answer was: Logbooks are actually notebooks, one and the same thing. So I -- we don't have any problem with it, Mr. Ostojic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Line 12 and 13 is the answer of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. At this point I wanted the witness to reference specific information that's on the map. We're in open session, right? Can we go to private session for a moment?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Let's go to private session for a short while.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So we are back in open session. The witness will be asked to indicate some locations on the map which is on the screen behind him.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, could you please -- well, first let me ask you: How is it that this map came into existence?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-131
utterances.text: This map was created in 1998. It was created by me and my colleagues based on the analyses performed from 1995, because at that time we had an analysis performed every month in writing. So it was sufficient for us to take the piece of paper. We knew the location. We knew everything else. We just needed to copy down frequencies, code-names, and which communications were operative at which times.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Did you create this map for the benefit of the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-131
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And is the information that's contained in the map information that you had at your disposal in 1995?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-131
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And was that the source of the information that was used to create the map?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-131
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. I guess just for the record the map has a 65 ter number, 1468. And I would ask the witness at this time to tell us a little bit about the map, if you would. Could you tell us what the symbols are that you used to create this map?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-131
utterances.text: The symbols we used are those that we used in the former JNA. I'm referring to the symbols used for radio relay hubs. Our task was to fill up the empty communication documents. So we would produce a form, blank one, and then as we gathered data we filled up the blank. That is to say, the command, deputy commander, and logistics assistant, and so on. Everybody had their own number, and we had a list of those numbers so that we would know. If somebody called, we would know what person called.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Could you just show us by indicating on the map where these radio relay hubs are located?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-131
utterances.text: You mean ours or --

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Maybe theirs. The VRS radio relay hubs, if you could.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-131
utterances.text: I don't even have to turn to the map, because I know by heart. These locations -- I will repeat once again what I said earlier. The army of Republika Srpska or, rather, the former JNA used the grid system. In that grid system, the facilities where we worked were also included in it. They had remained in our territory, and they had to do certain redirections, redirection of their communications. So it went from Cer to Vucevo to Brcko, Trebova, Svinjar, Banja Luka, and further on to Kozara. This was the western wing. As for the south wing, it went from Gucevo, Cero, towards Veliki Zep, because Veliki Zep was a kind of an intersection. That means that all of the most important communication lines of the army of Republika Srpska went across Veliki Zep. It was a purpose-built facility built long time before the war, and underneath it there were tunnels for communications in case of war. It was originally built by the JNA. Therefore, it was not a problem. The main problem for us was initially to uncover secret codes and frequencies, and after that everything went easy. The army of Republika Srpska used in parallel military equipment, but there was also civilian communications originating from these radio relay hubs and they were interconnected via SMC system which had a much greater number of channels and we were unable to monitor them.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Well, just for the benefit of the Court so that the Court can have a kind of overview of what you're talking about, could you actually point to some of these locations on the map so that they can -- so that the Court and all of us here can see the inter-relationship between these various points.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. How difficult is it to upload this map on e-court? Because if we could upload it -- yes. If we could upload it, then perhaps he can mark -- mark on it with the stylus and we can preserve it that way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think it's good enough. I think it's good enough. If we -- first gives us an indication -- Mr. Vanderpuye, if the witness more or less from here we can visualise the map, also the markings that there are on it. I mean, if he points at particular parts of that map, I'm sure that our staff can follow and zoom on that part as far as we can zoom, because I understand because the pixel grading amount does create a bit of a problem. But we could give it a try, because then he can mark on what he sees on his monitor with the stylus and we can preserve that as an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: That's fine as well. I'm just not familiar with the technical aspects of displaying the exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But I still agree with you. First he needs to point to the various parts on the map and then we try and zoom on those parts.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Did you follow me, Witness? You understand what -- what I would require you to do? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. Could you just indicate on the map by pointing to it, if you can, the relay -- radio relay hubs that you were referring to previously.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-131
utterances.text: This way. There were two branches, and I will start from the east. From Avala all the routes were picked up by the Cer hub, which was called Brana at the time. One wing of these communications went under the east corps to Bijeljina, Brcko, across Trebova, Svinjari, on to Kozara and Banja Luka. That's the 1st Krajina Corps. The southern wing had the following important relay hubs --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's stop there for the time being. Sit down, please. Usher, have you more or less figured out the point that he was pointing to, and if we could zoom on that. Yes. It's this point in the extreme -- extreme -- can we zoom more? No. It's the section -- it's the extreme right. Yes. It's the point that you have to zoom in where the lines start. Yes, exact. Not there. No, no. Yeah. You need to zoom in the section where all the lines -- it's -- just one more. Yes. Okay. We can start with that. Thanks. Now, Witness, you see a focal point there from which -- or from where lines are drawn, and I can read there Brana, Brana. Is that the point that you were referring us to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. That's one of the hubs of -- on the route from Belgrade to Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Can you circle --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Can you circle that point in red, please, or with the stylus?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Marks].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is the code-name for the Eastern Bosnian Corps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Now, you were explaining to us the direction of the two perpendicular lines to the left of that focal point. Can you explain to us what those two lines -- or where those two lines take us to, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] These lines were imaginary aerial lines showing the route, where it goes. If you take the airways for planes, there had to be optical visibility between two stations and there had to be a certain distance along which they can operate. The first line, the topmost line is the radio relay route connecting Bijeljina and Brcko. The second route is the SMC route, I believe, which directly went to Trebova, Svinjari, and on to Banja Luka, from Cer. And there is the third route which connects the terminal radio relay station which was the command of one of the brigades at Majevica in the territory of Brcko municipality.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Stop there. Just to make clear which is the third route, is it the one that is immediately beneath the second and which takes us to a triangle below which -- underneath which are the words Kalimbro?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Let's try to make it even clearer. Could I ask you to put against the first line number 1, against the second number 2, and against the third number 3, please, in that order.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Marks].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. You -- Mr. Vanderpuye, I don't know if you want to continue asking or whether he can proceed to explain to us what the other lines are, imaginary lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: We can proceed. The map is really only intended as a kind of general aid.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. So thank you, sir. Let's continue the -- describing the imaginary lines that are projected from the focal point Brana that you circled earlier on, and let's take the next line, the one where we see the numbers 859, 200 and whatever, and you can mark it as number 4 and then describe it to us, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Line number 4 is radio relay route between the command of the East Bosnia Corps and one of the Majevica Brigade -- brigades. I believe that it was the 2nd Majevica Brigade, if my memory doesn't fail me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And number 5?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Again, the route connecting this point with one of the Majevica brigades. These communications were up because there were no wire communication links. These were sites on elevated ground and mountains.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And the line which goes the other direction, SMC, 300, 200, which you can mark number 6.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This route linked the Cer site in Serbia and the East Bosnia Corps. SMC is a device with several channels which was used by civilian structures. This was the lifeline for communications covering Western Bosnia. In addition to the SMC, we have the number 800 there, which means that the military device RRU 800 was also used for military purposes. It went beyond Cer to Veliki Zep and Avala.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: My suggestion, but please advise me on this, is to -- for the time being focus on this map, have the witness put PW-131 against it, and that will be the first map. Then Madam Usher will come back, zoom out a little bit, and we move to the top of the triangle -- top of the curve that we have, and then the witness can be asked to start describing from there onwards. Okay. So, Witness, with the same stylus, please, on the top right-hand corner, could you put PW-131, please. I have his right number, correct number, don't I, 131?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Because incidentally, Borovcanin Defence, team you filed an explanation note in relation to the previous witness, but you have indicated him with the number PW-131 when it's PW-132. So you need to correct that. Okay? All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: To understand the geography better, could you underline Bijeljina, please? Is Bijeljina seen in this map, Mr. Witness? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Marks]. Yes. I can explain this. Bijeljina or, rather, East Bosnia Corps there had wire connections with Brana. Brana was located in a village and according to our information it was in one of the granaries there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Near Brcko.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, where it says Brana radio relay hub. They had to place it on elevated ground because this area is the area of plains.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Now, usher, you need to move -- thank you, Judge Kwon. You need to move and zoom in the top of the triangle. Okay. I have done it on my monitor. Bring it down a little bit -- no -- yes. Move it to the right slightly, and zoom in on the top of the triangle. That's enough. Thank you. Now, Witness, you see that we have the continuation -- partly the continuation of the first two lines, what you marked as 1 and 2 before. Now, on -- before we reach to the tip of the triangle, on the first line there are the numbers 12/800. Could you explain those to us? I'm sorry I've taken him over a little bit from you, but it's all for a good cause.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will do my best. The marking 12/800 stands for the following: The army of Republika Srpska used a military device RRU 800 for this route but only its 12 channels. It might also stand -- the marking might also stand as 24/800. In that case, 24 channels are used, and the flow of information is greater. However, in this particular instance, they used a 12-channel RRU 800.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. And in what is line number 2 that you had indicated to us before. Again we see the letters SMC, FM-200. If you could explain that, please, to us. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is the continuation of the route which led from Cer to Bijeljina in that this route goes directly from Bijeljina to the relay hub of Trebova. The SMC is the civilian device of communication, whereas the FM-200 is a military device. So this was an alternative bridge. All the units up to the level of brigade mostly ended up with radio relay communications -- mostly used radio relay communications.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. And just immediately below that, beneath that line, there are words that you can perhaps read for us giving us the benefit of having them translated to us into English and French.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It says below that the route was set up after the NATO strikes. This way we confirmed the information we came by. During the strikes, NATO destroyed the Cer facility, Svinjari facility, and the terminal relay station of Kozara in order to disrupt their communications system. Kozara was very important because that is where the most outlining radar of the army of Republika Srpska was which was also used by the Yugoslav Army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And a question which probably has a very obvious answer to it: We see on this map a curvature with interrupted or intermittent red lines. What's that supposed to indicate?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This red intermittent line was the front line between the ABiH and the army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I also notice on the map triangles in black and triangles in red with -- some of which are -- the red ones are flagged with numbers. Can you explain to us what's the difference between black triangles and red triangles and what the flagged part of the red triangles is supposed to signify, to indicate?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On the right-hand side we see the first red triangle and the red flag, which was something that the JNA or the VRS used to designate their units. So this is the command post of the Brcko Brigade. That's the first triangle. The second triangle with a flag as well stood for Tactical Group 5. I remember this well because the 1st Krajina Corps brought its units over to that spot, and that's where they had their provisional command, and it was called Tactical Group 5. The black markings, the black triangles under the JNA standards were designations for communications facilities, and that's how one would denote them, by drawing black triangles.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, we -- could you kindly put again number 1 against the line which you have already indicated in the previous image as number 1 and number 2 against the line which you have indicated previously as number 2.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Marks].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Now, going -- taking you back to the tip of the triangle, there is a line which runs perpendicular towards the west -- towards the left, sorry, towards the left. Could you give that line number 7, please. Mark it with number 7.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Marks].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, no, no. Usher, you need to help him cancel that number 7. What I meant is go to the tip of the triangle where there is Bozur. Now, I want you to concentrate on the line that from Bozur takes us from the left of the screen.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now I understand. But let me explain that this is the same route but -- it's the same route but it's just another station that was used for range. It's Bozur, and they had 12 channels there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So could you put again number 1 against that part of the -- of the route, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Marks].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Now, let's see. Now, I see that lines -- the continuation of line 1 and line 2 at the extreme left of the screen seem to converge at a place which on the map is described as Obala. Can you explain to us what that is? You can put a circle at the -- where -- on the place where they converge, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is the radio relay hub at Trebova. Now, why do these lines go up and this one goes down? For the simple reason that the range of the SMC device is far greater so that you could directly reach Banja Luka, whereas the radio relay device has a much shorter range, to the maximum of --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat the number of kilometres.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. The interpreters haven't caught the number of kilometres that you mentioned.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said that the RRU 800 has the maximum range of up to 80 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Perhaps you can now top right-hand corner of this map put your number, witness number, PW-131, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Marks].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We can store that, and Madam Usher can come forward again, and let's move to the other part of the map, further -- further west from -- you need to put the place where those two lines converge in the middle and zoom on that spot, the -- yes. I think it's enough. It's enough like that. It's enough like that. So now we come to the other part. You see that from the spot where these lines -- those previously two lines converge, 1 and 2, another two lines are projected. Would the one on top where we find FM-200 be still a continuation of line 1, or is it a new line?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. It's the continuation of line number 1, which goes to the radio relay station of Svinjari above Teslic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Could you kindly put number is against it where the river is. Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Marks].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And the line that goes south to Brana, I think it's --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is the line which has the route toward Doboj or what was the Operations Group Doboj at the time. Since Doboj is down in a depression, there was no optical visibility. You can see here that there is the terminal radio relay station to the west of the town of Doboj which was next to Ciganiste, and Ciganiste is close to the war zone, and this was an area that you could see from the place where we were with the naked eye. This was the link between the 1st Corps and Doboj and the Ozren units.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. So let's give it number 7, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Marks].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And again put PW-131, top right-hand corner, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Marks].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Now, registrar -- okay. Do that first. You need to focus now extreme right, the last two lines. Just below where we started from. Keep on going. Now take it up. Move it upward. No, that's the other way. Move -- yes, at -- and we need to concentrate on where those words are, Ka Avali. More or less. Now, Witness, you see again the focal point and the triangle marked against the words Ka Avali, and there are two lines that project from that spot towards the south. Let's take the first one. Where does this take us?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The first line, I can't see it here on the map, but I believe that it leads to Zvornik and the Zvornik Brigade. The second line runs directly to Veliki Zep. This is the second artery of the communications system, and that is why Cer was very important, and that was why NATO destroyed it right away at the time of the bombardment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So let's mark the first one with number 8 and the second with number 9.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Marks].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And again your PW-131 on the top.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Marks].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And I think we have a pretty clear picture now of all the map. You can store it. One moment, unless -- unless, Mr. Vanderpuye -- let's store it. Let's store it, and then we can go to any one of these maps as it becomes necessary. I think it will help us eliminate a lot of questions that I would have anticipated from the Defence bench. Back in your good hands.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Could you just indicate to us where Cer is located, Mr. Witness?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Your microphone.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Could you just, for the record, write the name Cer right next to that circle, please.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-131
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: You indicated previously that was the lifeline of communications for the VRS in Western Bosnia; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-131
utterances.text: I meant the radio relay communications. In view of the fact that they lost the Konjuh facility or -- excuse me. They lost the facilities from which we surveilled them. They had to re-route themselves in order to rely on such hubs in Serbia. There were some facilities that they used in the southern part as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Would it be convenient for you, Mr. Vanderpuye, to have the break now?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Yes, it would.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. So we'll have 30 minutes starting from now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We can continue, I suppose, Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I think the last I left off the witness had just circled the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Last point, Ka Avali.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: That's correct, indicating the town of Cer. Also he had indicated previously that there was some sort of an air-strike or bombing, I think is what the witness testified to.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And I just wondered if you could just tell us which bombing you were talking about or approximately when that happened.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-131
utterances.text: I was referring to the NATO bombing of the hubs in Serbia and certain facilities. We saw that with the naked eye. They destroyed Svinjar, destroyed the facilities at Ozren, Cer, Kozara. They also targeted Veliki Zep. This was when NATO ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What's the problem?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I think we've lost the last half of the translation maybe.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The witness did not finish the sentence, interpreters note.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So you are saying, Witness, we saw that with the naked eye. They destroyed Svinjar, destroyed the facilities at Ozren, Cer, Kozara. They also targeted Veliki Zep. This was when NATO, and you were about to continue when we didn't hear you anymore.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was going to say that this confirmed our knowledge about these being key facilities through which relay routes went.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
